lessons.title: Commodity Supercycles: Oil, Gold, and Metals

body.text: Commodities have the most violent cycles of any major asset, because demand can jump within a few years while new supply takes a decade to build. For India, which imports most of its oil and loves gold, those cycles flow straight into inflation, the rupee and which sectors win on Dalal Street.

children.text: Chapters 2 and 3 kept running into commodities: the oil shocks of the 1970s, the $147 oil of 2008, the gold imports that pushed India into the Fragile Five in 2013. This chapter looks at cycles outside the stock market that drive what happens inside it. We start with commodities, because their cycles are the easiest to see and the hardest to sit through. Shares represent businesses that can adapt. A barrel of oil or a tonne of copper cannot. Its price depends entirely on supply and demand, and both respond slowly.

markDefs.definition: A long period, often a decade or more, in which prices across many commodities rise well above their trend, usually because a large economy industrialises faster than new supply can be developed, followed by a long period of falling or weak prices.

children.text: starts when demand grows faster than anyone planned for, usually because a big economy builds cities, factories and infrastructure at speed. Supply cannot respond quickly: a new copper mine can take ten years or more from discovery to production, and a new oilfield or steel plant several years. So prices climb for years. High prices then trigger a wave of investment in new supply, and when that supply finally arrives, often just as demand slows, prices collapse. Producers cut investment, and the stage is set for the next shortage. Traders sum it up in a phrase: the cure for high prices is high prices.

body.caption: The stages of a commodity cycle

cells: Years of low prices have made producers cut spending on new mines, wells and plants
Commodity stocks are cheap, unloved and ignored
A big economy industrialises, or a shock disrupts supply, and existing capacity runs out
Prices rise sharply, and producers' profits jump
High prices make new projects look irresistible, and companies borrow to expand
Record profits, low P/Es, and talk of a new era of permanent scarcity
New supply arrives, often just as demand slows, and prices collapse
Profits vanish, heavily borrowed producers struggle, and stocks fall far more than the index

body.title: Crude oil price at major turning points, US dollars per barrel (approximate, not inflation-adjusted)

children.text: Every major swing on this chart came from the pattern above. The 1970s shocks triggered huge new drilling in the North Sea, Alaska and Mexico, and by 1986 oil had collapsed. China's boom drove oil to $147 in July 2008; the global crisis cut it by about three quarters within five months. High prices from 2011 to 2014 funded the US shale revolution, which roughly doubled US crude output in about seven years, and when OPEC decided in November 2014 not to cut production, prices fell about 76% by January 2016. In April 2020, with COVID lockdowns emptying roads and storage tanks full, the US WTI benchmark briefly traded below zero. Less than two years later, after Russia invaded Ukraine, Brent crude touched about $139.

body.title: Who wins and who loses in India when crude oil rises

columns.label: Usually hurt
points: The rupee and the current account deficit, since India pays for oil in dollars
Inflation, through fuel, transport and fertiliser costs, which can push the RBI to raise rates
Paint, tyre and chemical companies that use crude-based raw materials
Airlines, where fuel is one of the largest costs
Oil marketing companies such as IOC, BPCL and HPCL, when they cannot pass on price rises quickly

columns.label: Usually helped
points: Upstream producers such as ONGC and Oil India, which sell the crude
The government's receipts from oil producers, though subsidies and pressure to cut fuel taxes can offset this
Gulf remittances to India, as oil-exporting economies grow richer
Some energy-related capital goods and services companies

body.text: The oil crash of 2014 to 2016 was one of the luckiest breaks the Indian economy has had. Petrol prices had been freed in 2010 and diesel in October 2014, so falling crude could have flowed straight to consumers. Instead, the government raised excise duty on petrol and diesel nine times between November 2014 and January 2016, capturing much of the windfall for its budget. At the same time the current account deficit shrank sharply and inflation fell, which helped the RBI cut rates and let the reform agenda of Lesson 3.5 begin on a stable footing.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: Crude oil falls from $110 to $55 a barrel and stays there for a year. Which combination is most likely for India?
options: Higher inflation, a weaker rupee and pressure on the RBI to raise rates
Lower inflation, a smaller current account deficit, a more stable rupee and room for the RBI to cut rates
No effect, because India produces most of its own oil
Higher profits for ONGC and lower profits for paint companies
body.explanation: India imports more than 85% of its crude, so a lower oil price cuts the import bill, shrinks the current account deficit, eases pressure on the rupee and lowers inflation. That combination gives the RBI room to cut rates. Paint companies usually benefit from cheaper crude-linked raw materials, while upstream producers like ONGC earn less, the reverse of option D.

children.text: Gold: The Fear and Real Interest Rate Cycle

body.title: Gold price at major turning points, US dollars per ounce (approximate, not inflation-adjusted)

markDefs.definition: The interest rate after subtracting inflation. If a bond pays 7% and inflation is 5%, the real rate is roughly 2%.

children.text: Gold is not really an industrial commodity. Most of it is held as jewellery, bars, coins and central bank reserves, and it pays no interest or dividend. Its cycle is driven less by mines and factories than by fear, the US dollar and, above all,

. When inflation is high and deposits and bonds pay less than inflation, holding gold costs nothing in lost income, and it soars, as in the 1970s and after 2008. When real rates are high and positive, as in the 1980s and 1990s, gold slumps for years. Since 2022, central banks around the world, including the RBI, have bought gold at the fastest pace in decades, more than 1,000 tonnes a year from 2022 to 2024, adding a new source of demand.

body.label: Gold's own lost decades
body.value: About 28 years to regain its 1980 high
body.context: Gold peaked near $850 an ounce in January 1980, fell about 70% to around $253 by July 1999, and did not rise above $850 again until January 2008. Like the Nikkei in Lesson 2.4, the asset everyone wanted at the top of one cycle went nowhere for a generation.

body.text: Indian investors experience a smoother gold cycle than the dollar chart suggests. Gold is priced in dollars, so when the rupee weakens, the rupee price of gold rises even if the dollar price does not. In 2013, for example, dollar gold fell sharply, but the collapse of the rupee cushioned much of that fall for Indian buyers. Over long periods, rupee depreciation has added meaningfully to gold's returns in India, which is part of why Indian households trust it so much. It still has long, flat stretches: rupee gold was lower at the end of 2015 than in 2012.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Gold's January 1980 high of about $850 an ounce was not exceeded again until the year ___.
body.explanation: Gold rose above $850 in January 2008, 28 years later. In inflation-adjusted terms, the 1980 peak was not surpassed until much more recently. Buying any asset at the top of a mania, whether gold in 1980, the Nikkei in 1989 or the Sensex in 1992, can cost decades of returns.

children.text: Metals: The Most Cyclical Stocks on Dalal Street

Industrial metals such as steel, copper, aluminium and zinc follow global construction and manufacturing, and for the last 25 years that has mostly meant China, which produces more than half the world's steel. The 2000s China boom sent metal prices and Indian metal stocks such as Tata Steel, Hindalco, JSW Steel, SAIL and Vedanta soaring, and many Indian steelmakers borrowed heavily to expand, including through large overseas acquisitions. When Chinese growth slowed after 2011 and its steel mills began exporting their surplus, prices and profits collapsed, culminating in the commodity bust of 2015 to 2016. The Nifty Metal index has been one of the most volatile sector indices on NSE.

markDefs.definition: A company whose profits rise and fall sharply with the economic or commodity cycle, such as a steel, cement, metals or auto company, as opposed to a defensive company like a consumer staples maker whose profits are steadier.

children.text: Metals teach the most counterintuitive valuation lesson in investing. For a

, the P/E ratio often looks lowest at the top of the cycle, when earnings are at a peak that will not last, and highest at the bottom, when earnings have collapsed. Buying a metal stock because its P/E is 5 can mean buying at exactly the wrong moment.

body.caption: The P/E paradox: a hypothetical steel company at the top and bottom of a cycle

cells: Earnings fall, and the price halves
Earnings recover, and the price can multiply

body.title: Find the Missing P/E
body.prompt: Using the table above, what is the steel company's P/E at the bottom of the cycle, with a share price of ₹240 and EPS of ₹10?
body.explanation: P/E = ₹240 ÷ ₹10 = 24. At the top, the P/E was ₹480 ÷ ₹80 = 6. The share price halved, but earnings fell 87.5%, so the P/E quadrupled. A screener sorted by low P/E would have flagged this stock as a bargain at the top and as expensive at the bottom, exactly backwards. For cyclicals, investors often look instead at price to book value, or at earnings averaged across a full cycle.

body.text: Commodity cycles can be brutal even for new-economy materials. Lithium, essential for electric vehicle batteries, was described as the new oil when prices in China soared about tenfold between 2020 and late 2022. Miners worldwide rushed to expand, EV demand grew more slowly than hoped, and prices fell by more than 80% within about a year. A real long-term story, the energy transition, did not stop a classic boom and bust in the price.

children.text: Using Commodity Cycles as an Investor

body.title: Questions to Ask Before Buying a Commodity or Commodity Stock
steps: Are current profits and prices well above their long-run average, suggesting you are near a peak rather than a trough?
Are producers announcing big new capacity additions, the classic sign that oversupply is a few years away?
How much debt has the company taken on to expand during the good years?
What is happening to demand in China, the world's largest consumer of most metals?
Is the US dollar strengthening, which usually pressures commodity prices, or weakening?
For gold, are real interest rates rising or falling?
Are you judging a cyclical company on peak earnings P/E, or on earnings across a full cycle and price to book value?

body.title: The Record-Profit Steel Stock
body.scenario: It is April 2022. Steel and metal prices are near record highs after the post-COVID recovery and the Russia-Ukraine war. Tata Steel has just reported the highest annual profit in its history, and several Indian steelmakers trade at P/E ratios of around 4 to 6. A friend in Jamshedpur says: "The Nifty trades at a P/E above 20 and these steel companies are at 5. It's the cheapest sector in the market. I'm putting my whole bonus into metal stocks."
body.prompt: Using this lesson, what is your friend missing?
body.modelAnswer: Your friend is applying a non-cyclical valuation rule to a cyclical sector at what looks like the top of its cycle. Record steel prices, driven by a demand rebound and a war-related supply shock, produced record profits, which is exactly why the P/E looks low. If prices normalise, earnings can fall far more than the share price, and the P/E will rise even as the stock falls. Several warning signs from the checklist are present: prices and profits far above their long-run average, a supply shock that could fade, and the RBI and other central banks about to raise rates, which slows construction and manufacturing. In fact, metal prices and Indian metal stocks fell sharply in the months that followed as global rate hikes began, and Tata Steel's consolidated profit fell by roughly 80% from FY22 to FY23. A cycle-aware investor would look at earnings averaged over a full cycle, check price to book value against history, avoid putting a whole bonus into one of the market's most volatile sectors, and treat record profits in a commodity business as a reason for caution, not confidence.

cards.definition: A decade-plus rise in commodity prices well above trend, driven by industrialisation outpacing supply, followed by a long bust.

cards.definition: High prices encourage new supply and reduce demand, which eventually brings prices down.
The rapid growth of US oil production from shale rock after about 2008, which helped cause the 2014 to 2016 oil price collapse.
The interest rate minus inflation. Falling or negative real rates tend to support gold, while high positive real rates weigh on it.
A company whose profits swing sharply with the economic or commodity cycle, such as steel, metals, cement or autos.

body.label: PPAC: Indian Basket Crude Oil Prices
body.description: The Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas publishes the price of the Indian basket of crude oil, import data and domestic fuel prices. Track it alongside the rupee and CPI inflation to see how the oil cycle feeds into India's economy.

children.text: Oil pushes up inflation, inflation pushes the RBI to raise rates, and rates change what every other asset is worth. Lesson 4.2 follows that chain to its centre: India's interest rate cycles, bond yields and what they do to equity valuations.

body.text: Commodity prices in this lesson are approximate, rounded and not adjusted for inflation, and figures after mid 2025 are not covered. The steel company table is hypothetical. References to companies describe historical events for education only. Commodity and commodity-linked investments can be highly volatile, and nothing here is a recommendation or investment advice.

points: Commodity supercycles happen because demand can surge within a few years while new supply takes a decade, and high prices always eventually trigger the oversupply that ends them
Oil swung from about $147 in July 2008 to $36 by December, from about $115 in 2014 to $27 in 2016, and below zero for US WTI in April 2020, before touching about $139 in 2022
India imports more than 85% of its crude, so oil cycles drive its inflation, rupee, current account deficit and RBI policy, and create clear sector winners and losers
Gold follows fear, the dollar and real interest rates rather than industrial demand, and took about 28 years to regain its 1980 high, though rupee weakness has smoothed its cycle for Indian buyers
Metal stocks are among the most cyclical on NSE, and their P/E looks lowest at the top of the cycle and highest at the bottom
Record profits and low P/Es in a commodity business are often a sign of a peak, not a bargain
